analysis.one_liner: Rolls back federal banking rules on consumer disclosures, community lending reviews, and bank oversight.
analysis.headline: The House Banking Committee approved this bank deregulation bill on a narrow 27-23 vote in July 1995, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have loosened a long list of federal rules that apply to banks and other lenders. It would have repealed most of the Truth in Savings Act's requirements that banks clearly disclose interest rates and fees on deposit accounts, let banks share customer information freely across their affiliates, shrink the scope of the Community Reinvestment Act, which pushes banks to lend in lower-income neighborhoods, and cut back mortgage disclosure rules and borrowers' ability to cancel certain refinancing deals. It would also have eased approval requirements for bank mergers and removed some reporting rules on loans that banks make to their own executives. The House Banking Committee approved it 27-23, but it never came to a vote by the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, savings institutions, credit card banks, and other deposit-taking lenders, which would face fewer disclosure mandates, lighter community reinvestment scrutiny, faster regulatory approvals for mergers and new branches, and less reporting on insider loans. Bank executives and directors also gain, through repeal of reporting requirements on loans banks make to their own officers and looser limits on dual directorships.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals most Truth in Savings Act disclosure rules, including requirements that banks provide rate and fee schedules and itemize interest earned and fees charged on periodic statements [S2][S3][S4]
Allows banks to freely share customer information among affiliates, with only a notice and an opt-out for the customer [S3][S4]

Exempts banks with $100 million or less in assets from Community Reinvestment Act examinations and lets banks with up to $250 million self-certify their own compliance instead of being examined [S2][S3][S4]

Prohibits regulators from requiring banks to collect or report loan data under the Community Reinvestment Act, and forbids rules that would push banks to serve all segments of their community [S3][S4]

Exempts loans to executive officers made through widely available employee benefit programs from insider-lending restrictions, and repeals requirements that banks report loans to their own executives and major shareholders [S2][S3]

Lets banks with $250 million or less in assets face mandatory on-site examinations every 18 to 24 months instead of annually, and allows well-capitalized banks to merge, open branches, and add ATMs without prior regulatory approval [S2][S3]

Limits banks' and creditors' liability under the Truth in Lending Act for certain finance-charge disclosure errors and denies a right of rescission on some refinancings of a principal dwelling [S2][S3][S4]

analysis.who_pays: Bank customers, who would get less information about the rates, fees, and penalties attached to their accounts and about the true cost of mortgage credit; residents of lower-income neighborhoods, who would lose leverage under a weakened Community Reinvestment Act; and borrowers, who would have fewer ways to challenge inaccurate or missing loan disclosures.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Truth in Savings disclosure requirements, including the annual percentage yield definition and civil liability for noncompliance, would make it harder for consumers to compare accounts and to enforce accurate rate and fee information [S2][S3]

Exempting small banks from CRA examinations and letting mid-size banks self-certify, while barring regulators from requiring loan data collection, would reduce public visibility into whether banks are meeting the credit needs of their communities [S2][S3]

The bill's deregulatory premise has a cost side supporters had to acknowledge: weaker disclosure, weaker community lending reviews, and looser oversight of bank insider lending and mergers remove checks that existed because disclosure rules alone had not prevented past problems [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers banks real compliance savings, and a few of its provisions do help consumers directly, such as requiring banks to pay interest on the full daily balance of a deposit account, giving mortgage applicants a promise that quoted note rates and points will be honored, and letting creditors count community-development lending anywhere in the country toward their CRA record [S3][S4]. But the bulk of the bill is a one-way transfer: nearly every disclosure, examination, and reporting requirement it removes is one that exists for the benefit of depositors, mortgage borrowers, and lower-income communities, and several provisions shield bank insiders from scrutiny. Taken as a whole, the consumer gains are small relative to the protections given up.

outcome.mechanism: The House Banking Committee reported the bill to the floor on a narrow 27-23 vote, where it sat on the House calendar for nearly a year and a half and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative James Leach introduced the bill on June 15, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services [S1][S6]
The committee held markup sessions on four days between June 21 and June 28, 1995, and ordered the bill reported on a 27-23 roll-call vote [S6]
The committee reported the bill with amendments on July 18, 1995, as H. Rept. 104-193, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 98 [S6][S4]
On June 18, 1996, the committee filed a supplemental report on the bill, which was the last recorded action [S6]
The bill never received a vote by the full House and died at the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997 [S1][S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bank customers, mortgage borrowers, and community groups that count on public CRA ratings kept the disclosure and community-lending rules the bill would have weakened; banks did not get the regulatory relief they sought.

for.name: Rep. James A. Leach
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee markup, and later asked unanimous consent to file a supplemental committee report

for.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee majority
for.role: 27 committee members voting to report the bill
for.what_they_did: Voted 27-23 in markup to order the bill reported to the House with amendments

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee minority
against.role: 23 committee members voting against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted no in committee markup on the motion to order the bill reported

against.name: House leadership (unidentified in the record)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote during the remainder of the 104th Congress, leaving it on the calendar until the Congress expired

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only the raw 27-23 committee vote to report the bill and does not include the party breakdown of that vote, so the partisan shape of the committee fight cannot be confirmed from the record; the bill itself never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip away disclosure, examination, and reporting requirements that exist mainly to inform depositors and borrowers and to push banks to serve lower-income communities; its main benefit to banks comes at the direct expense of the transparency those customers rely on.

industries.industry: Credit card banks, trust banks, and wholesale lenders
industries.note: As 'special purpose institutions' that take no small retail deposits, they would be deemed to satisfy Community Reinvestment Act requirements despite serving no local community, effectively exempting them from the law's purpose.

industries.industry: Bank executives, directors, and holding companies
industries.note: The bill repeals reporting of loans banks make to their own officers and major shareholders, permits preferential insider loans under employee benefit programs, loosens interlock limits on directors serving competing institutions, and raises the ceiling on unapproved credit union insider loans from $10,000 to $50,000.

industries.industry: Community development and consumer advocacy organizations
industries.note: The CRA changes, including self-certification, examination exemptions, a ban on new loan-data collection, and conclusive ratings with limited reconsideration, would cut the public information and leverage these groups use to challenge banks that neglect lower-income neighborhoods.
